title: What is the difference between a single shared database and the database-per-service approach?

s1_definition.profdef: A single shared database is one physical database that many services read from and write to directly, so the schema becomes a public contract coupling every service together. The database-per-service pattern gives each microservice its own private database that only that service accesses directly; other services obtain or change the data exclusively through the owning service's API or by consuming its events. Shared database is simpler and preserves ACID transactions and joins across data but tightly couples teams and deployments; database-per-service decouples teams, enables independent deployment and polyglot storage, and provides fault isolation, at the cost of losing cross-service joins and distributed transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one giant master ledger book that every department writes into at the same time. If the accounts team changes a column heading, the loans team's entries break; if two departments grab the book at once there is contention; and if the book is dropped, the whole bank stops. That is a shared database. Now imagine each department keeps its own private ledger locked in its own cabinet, and when the loans team needs Rajesh's balance they phone the accounts team and ask, rather than reaching into their cabinet. That is database-per-service — slower to ask around, but no department can break another's records, and each can reorganize its own cabinet freely.
s1_definition.oneliner: A shared database couples everyone through one schema and one failure point; database-per-service gives each service a private store it fully owns and others reach only through its API.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A single shared database is one physical database that many services read from and write to directly, so the schema becomes a public contract coupling every service together. The database-per-service pattern gives each microservice its own private database that only that service accesses directly; other services obtain or change the data exclusively through the owning service's API or by consuming its events. Shared database is simpler and preserves ACID transactions and joins across data but tightly couples teams and deployments; database-per-service decouples teams, enables independent deployment and polyglot storage, and provides fault isolation, at the cost of losing cross-service joins and distributed transactions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps one giant master ledger book that every department writes into at the same time. If the accounts team changes a column heading, the loans team's entries break; if two departments grab the book at once there is contention; and if the book is dropped, the whole bank stops. That is a shared database. Now imagine each department keeps its own private ledger locked in its own cabinet, and when the loans team needs Rajesh's balance they phone the accounts team and ask, rather than reaching into their cabinet. That is database-per-service — slower to ask around, but no department can break another's records, and each can reorganize its own cabinet freely.

**One line to remember:** A shared database couples everyone through one schema and one failure point; database-per-service gives each service a private store it fully owns and others reach only through its API.

sections.s2_technical:
With a shared database, all services point at the same physical database and the same tables. The immediate appeal is real: you keep ACID transactions spanning entities (debit and credit in one commit), you can write a single SQL join across what would otherwise be separate domains, there is exactly one source of truth with no synchronization, and operationally there is one database to run. For a small system or a modular monolith this is often the pragmatic, correct choice, and I never pretend otherwise.

The problems appear as the system and the organization grow. The schema becomes a hidden shared contract: the accounts table is now used by the transfer service, the statement service, and the fraud service, so you cannot alter a column without risking breaking several services owned by different teams, and changes require cross-team coordination and lockstep deployments, which kills independent delivery. There is runtime coupling too — a heavy report query from one service can lock rows or saturate connections and degrade every other service, so there is no fault isolation. And you are forced into one engine for everyone, losing polyglot persistence. The shared database quietly becomes the single biggest coupler in your architecture even though the code is split into services.

With database-per-service, each service owns its data exclusively. The owning service is the only one that connects to that database, and the only way for others to touch the data is a well-defined API call or a published event. This yields loose coupling (the schema is now a private implementation detail the owning team can change freely), independent deployability (schema migrations affect only one service), fault isolation (one database's slowness or outage is contained), and polyglot persistence (each service uses the engine that fits its workload). This pattern is what actually makes a microservices architecture deliver on its promises.

The costs are equally real and you must name them. You lose cross-service joins — if the statement service needs account names from the account service, it calls the API, or it keeps a local read-optimized copy kept in sync by events (data replication via events, often materialized into a read model). You lose distributed ACID transactions — a business operation spanning two services can no longer be one commit, so you use the Saga pattern with compensating actions and accept eventual consistency. You take on more operational surface — more databases to run, back up, and monitor. And you must solve data consistency explicitly, typically with the transactional outbox pattern so a database write and an event publish cannot drift apart.

A senior engineer frames the choice as coupling versus simplicity. Start with a shared database or a modular monolith when the domain is small or unclear; adopt database-per-service when teams and services multiply and independent deployment and fault isolation become worth the added complexity of eventual consistency and inter-service data access. The anti-pattern to avoid is the worst of both worlds: splitting the code into microservices but leaving them all on one shared database — now you have distributed-system complexity and a shared coupler with none of the isolation benefits.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India has a transfer feature and a statement feature. The question is whether both should hit one shared accounts table or whether each service should own its own data.

Problem 1 — In the shared-database design, both the transfer service and the statement service read and write the same accounts table. When the statement team wants to rename a column, the transfer service breaks unless both deploy together. Worse, a heavy month-end statement query locks account rows and slows live transfers for Rajesh and Priya. This is the coupling and lack of fault isolation of a shared database.

Problem 2 — In the database-per-service design, the account service owns the balances exclusively. The statement service no longer reads the accounts table; instead it keeps its own local read model of balances, updated by consuming `AccountChangedEvent` events the account service publishes. Now the statement team can change its schema freely, its heavy queries run against its own database, and a statement-database slowdown cannot touch live transfers.

Problem 3 — The trade-off surfaces immediately: the statement service's local copy is eventually consistent. Right after a transfer, there is a brief window where the statement read model has not yet processed the event. We accept this for statements (a few seconds of staleness is fine) precisely because we would never accept it for the actual money, which stays in the account service under strong consistency.

What the code will do: a runnable demo contrasts both approaches side by side. `SharedDatabaseWorld` shows a single `AccountTable` written to directly by both `SharedTransferService` and `SharedStatementService`, and demonstrates the coupling by having a statement query observe and depend on the same rows. `PerServiceWorld` shows an `AccountService` owning its data and publishing events, and a `StatementService` with its own local read model updated only via those events, demonstrating ownership, the API/event boundary, and eventual consistency.

```bash
javac DbOwnershipDemo.java

mvn -pl account-service clean package
mvn -pl statement-service clean package

docker run -d --name pg-accounts   -e POSTGRES_DB=accountdb   -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name pg-statements -e POSTGRES_DB=statementdb -p 5433:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:3.7.0
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50000 from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), run first in the shared-database world and then in the database-per-service world.

Step 1 (shared): `SharedTransferService.transfer()` writes the one shared accounts table directly. Rajesh goes to Rs.950,000 and Priya to Rs.300,000 in that single table.

Step 2 (shared): `SharedStatementService.printBalance()` reads the exact same table. It sees Rs.950,000 immediately and strongly consistent, which looks nice, but it is reading rows owned by the transfer feature. A schema change by either team, or a heavy statement query, directly affects the other — tight coupling and no fault isolation.

Step 3 (per-service): `AccountService.transfer()` writes only its own private account database, committing with strong consistency. Rajesh goes to Rs.950,000 inside the account service's database, which nobody else can read directly.

Step 4 (per-service): The account service publishes two `AccountChangedEvent` facts. The statement service, subscribed to those events, updates its own local read model. The data has now crossed the service boundary as an event, not as a shared row.

Step 5 (per-service): `StatementService.printBalance()` reads its own read model, not the account service's database. It returns Rs.950,000, but note this value arrived via the event — there is a brief eventual-consistency window right after the transfer before the event is processed. We accept this for statements because the authoritative money lives in the account service and stays strongly consistent.

Final output:

```
11:30:00 INFO    ===== SHARED DATABASE (anti-pattern) =====
11:30:00 INFO    [SHARED] transfer done, wrote accounts table directly
11:30:00 INFO    [SHARED] statement reads shared table: SAV2001 = Rs.950000  (coupled: a schema change here breaks the transfer service too)
11:30:00 INFO    ===== DATABASE-PER-SERVICE =====
11:30:00 INFO    [ACCOUNT-SVC] transfer committed in OWN db (strong consistency)
11:30:00 INFO    [STATEMENT-SVC] reads OWN read model: SAV2001 = Rs.950000  (eventually consistent; decoupled from account-service schema)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The difference between a single shared database and database-per-service is really a difference in coupling. With a shared database, many services read and write the same physical database and the same tables, so the schema silently becomes a public contract binding every service and every team together. That buys you simplicity — you keep ACID transactions across entities, you can join across domains, there is one source of truth and one database to operate — and for a small system or a modular monolith it is often the right, honest choice. But as services and teams multiply, it becomes the single biggest coupler in the architecture: you cannot change a column without risking breaking other teams' services, changes force lockstep deployments, a heavy query in one service degrades every other service because there is no fault isolation, and you are stuck on one storage engine for everyone.

Database-per-service flips this. Each service privately owns its database, and the only way another service touches that data is through the owning service's API or by consuming its published events. This is what makes microservices actually deliver their promises: loose coupling, because the schema is now a private implementation detail the owning team can change freely; independent deployability, because a migration affects only one service; fault isolation, because one database's slowness or outage is contained; and polyglot persistence, because each service picks the engine that fits its workload. The honest costs are that I lose cross-service joins, so a service that needs another's data either calls its API or keeps a local read model kept fresh by events, and I lose distributed ACID transactions, so a business operation spanning services becomes a Saga with compensating actions and eventual consistency, plus more databases to operate and the dual-write problem to solve with an outbox.

I lived this at National Bank of India with our transfer and statement features. Under a shared database they both hit the same accounts table, so when the statement team wanted a schema change it threatened the transfer service, and month-end statement queries locked account rows and slowed live transfers for Rajesh and Priya. We moved to database-per-service: the account service owns the balances with strong consistency and publishes AccountChangedEvents, and the statement service stopped reading the accounts table entirely and instead keeps its own local read model updated from those events. After that the statement team could evolve its schema freely, its heavy queries ran against its own database, and a statement-database slowdown could no longer touch live money movement. The trade-off we accepted was that the statement balance is eventually consistent, with a brief window after a transfer before the event is applied, which is fine for reporting precisely because the authoritative money stays strongly consistent inside the account service.

The nuance I always add is how to choose. Start with a shared database or a modular monolith when the domain is small or the boundaries are unclear, and adopt database-per-service when independent deployment and fault isolation become worth the added complexity of eventual consistency. And I explicitly warn against the worst of both worlds: splitting the code into microservices while leaving them all on one shared database, which gives you all the distributed-system complexity with none of the isolation.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: a shared database couples every service through one schema and one failure point, while database-per-service gives each service a private store it fully owns and others reach only through its API or events, trading cross-service joins and distributed transactions for the loose coupling, independent deployability, and fault isolation that make microservices worthwhile.
